blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Confounding is a distortion of the exposure–outcome association by a third variable that is a common cause of both. Recall §11.6: a variable is a confounder if it (1) is associated with the exposure in the source population, (2) is a risk factor for the outcome (or a proxy for one) independently of the exposure, that is, among the unexposed, and (3) is not an effect of the exposure (not on the causal path). §11.6.1 refines this with the backdoor criterion.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
§11.6 and §11.7 built confounding and its removal by stratification. This section places it among the threats to validity and answers the design question left open there: what can a study do about confounding before any data are analysed?

Design-stage control. Three tools act before analysis:

  1. Randomisation: the investigator assigns exposure by chance, so measured and unmeasured confounders are balanced on average (recall §1.5; §15.9). Only available when the exposure can be assigned.
  2. Restriction: admit only people in one category of the confounder (for example, only rural PHCs, or only non-smokers). The confounder cannot vary, so it cannot confound. The cost is fewer eligible people and a narrower population for generalisation.
  3. Matching: choose comparison subjects with the same confounder values as each index subject (individually or by frequency). In a case-control study matching does not by itself remove confounding; the analysis must respect it (Rothman, Greenland & Lash, 2008; recall §10.8; §13.2.9 gives conditional logistic regression, a regression method for matched sets).

Analysis-stage control of measured confounders: stratification with Mantel–Haenszel (recall §11.7), standardisation (recall §7.4.2), multiple regression (recall §12.4; Chapters 13–14) and propensity scores (§15.3).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Recall §11.7: in the infant cohort, PHC confounded the association between not being EBF and diarrhoea (crude RR 3.54; MH RR 2.93). Three design alternatives would have handled it before analysis. Restriction to the rural PHC gives the stratum RR, 2.88. Frequency matching would have enrolled EBF and not-EBF infants in the same PHC proportions. Randomisation is not possible here: feeding cannot ethically be assigned. What none of these can do is remove a confounder nobody thought of, such as household wealth if it was never recorded. §17.3.1 asks how strong such a confounder would have to be.

points.html: Unmeasured confounding comes from a confounder never recorded; no analysis of the data at hand removes it. Residual confounding is what remains after adjusting for a measured confounder, because it was measured with error or grouped too coarsely (recall §11.6; Fewell et al., 2007). Better measurement shrinks residual confounding; only new data, or a sensitivity analysis (§17.3.1), address unmeasured confounding.
Confounding can push an estimate in either direction, including towards the null or across it (Simpson’s paradox, recall §11.7). A null result can hide a real effect.
A randomised trial can still be confounded by chance imbalance in a small trial, and can still be biased (§17.1.1).

blocks.html: Sensitivity and Quantitative Bias Analysis; the E-value

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A sensitivity analysis repeats an analysis under different plausible assumptions to see whether the conclusion changes. Quantitative bias analysis is the form that models a specific systematic error: it states the bias parameters (for example, the sensitivity and specificity of exposure measurement, or the strength of an unmeasured confounder) and computes the estimate those parameters imply. It “provides a quantitative estimate of the direction, magnitude and uncertainty arising from systematic errors” (Lash et al., 2014). The E-value is “the minimum strength of association, on the risk ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the treatment and the outcome to fully explain away a specific treatment-outcome association, conditional on the measured covariates” (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A confidence interval describes chance only. Bias analysis puts a number on the other two explanations. Two simple tools cover most needs.

  • Misclassification. If you can state the likely Se and Sp of your exposure measure (from a validation sub-study or the literature), the formula of §17.2.2 recovers the table you would have seen with perfect measurement.
  • Unmeasured confounding. Describe a hypothetical confounder U by two risk ratios: RR_EU, how much more common U is in the exposed than the unexposed, and RR_UD, how much U raises the risk of the outcome. The bounding factor B = RR_EU × RR_UD ÷ (RR_EU + RR_UD − 1) is the largest factor by which such a confounder could have inflated the observed RR (Ding & VanderWeele, 2016). Divide the observed RR and its confidence limits by B to get the smallest true RR compatible with that confounder. The E-value is the value of RR_EU = RR_UD that makes B equal to the observed RR.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
The E-value formula. Set RR_EU = RR_UD = x and ask when the bounding factor equals the observed RR:

  1. x² ÷ (2x − 1) = RR
  2. x² − 2RR·x + RR = 0
  3. x = RR ± √(RR² − RR). The larger root (the one above RR) is the relevant one:

E-value = RR + √[RR × (RR − 1)]

For an RR below 1, first take its inverse; “If the original risk ratio is below 1, then one first takes the inverse before applying the E-value formula” (Mathur et al., 2018). Compute it for the point estimate and for the confidence limit closer to the null (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017); if the interval already includes 1, the E-value for the limit is 1.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The infant cohort, after adjustment for PHC: RR_MH 2.93 (95% CI 1.60 to 5.35) (recall §11.7). A reviewer asks whether household wealth, which was not recorded, could explain the association.

blocks.alt: Curves of the confounder strengths that would explain away the point estimate and the lower confidence limit, with the E-values 5.31 and 2.59 on the diagonal and an assumed confounder of strength 2 and 2 below both curves
blocks.caption: Figure 17.2. Every pair (RR_EU, RR_UD) on or above the orange curve could explain away the MH RR of 2.93; on or above the blue curve, the lower confidence limit of 1.60. The E-values are where each curve crosses the diagonal.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. E-value for the point estimate: 2.930 + √(2.930 × 1.930) = 2.930 + √5.655 = 2.930 + 2.378 = 5.31.
  2. E-value for the lower limit (unrounded 1.604): 1.604 + √(1.604 × 0.604) = 1.604 + 0.984 = 2.59.
  3. Reading: to explain away the association entirely, an unmeasured confounder would need to be about 5.3 times as common among not-EBF infants and raise diarrhoea risk about 5.3-fold, beyond PHC. To pull the lower limit down to 1, both associations would need to reach about 2.6.
  4. A specific confounder: suppose poverty is twice as common among not-EBF infants (RR_EU = 2) and doubles diarrhoea risk (RR_UD = 2). B = (2 × 2) ÷ (2 + 2 − 1) = 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33. Corrected RR ≥ 2.930 ÷ 1.333 = 2.20, lower limit ≥ 1.604 ÷ 1.333 = 1.20. Such a confounder could not explain the association away.
  5. Misclassification: had the recorded table been the non-differential one of §17.2.2 (27.8/48.2 and 19.2/104.8) and the Se and Sp known to be 0.80 and 0.90, the correction gives a = (27.8 − 0.10 × 47) ÷ 0.70 = 23.1 ÷ 0.70 = 33.0 and b = (48.2 − 0.10 × 153) ÷ 0.70 = 32.9 ÷ 0.70 = 47.0: the true table, and RR 3.54, are recovered. With wrong assumed values (Se 0.90, Sp 0.95) the same calculation gives RR 2.77. The correction is only as good as the Se and Sp you feed it, which is why bias analyses report a range of values.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
d <- read.csv("data/ebf_diarrhoea_cohort.csv")
library(epiR)
tab <- xtabs(~ factor(not_ebf, levels = c(1, 0)) +
               factor(diarrhoea, levels = c(1, 0)) + phc, data = d)
mh <- epi.2by2(tab, method = "cohort.count")$massoc.detail$RR.mh.wald
mh

# E-value (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017): RR + sqrt(RR * (RR - 1))
evalue <- function(rr) {
  if (rr < 1) rr <- 1 / rr
  rr + sqrt(rr * (rr - 1))
}
c(point = evalue(mh$est), ci_limit = evalue(mh$lower))

# Bounding factor for an assumed confounder (Ding & VanderWeele, 2016)
bf <- function(rr_eu, rr_ud) rr_eu * rr_ud / (rr_eu + rr_ud - 1)
round(unlist(mh) / bf(2, 2), 2)

# Simple bias analysis: back-correct a misclassified exposure
correct <- function(x_obs, n, se, sp)
  (x_obs - (1 - sp) * n) / (se + sp - 1)
# observed 2x2 (Se 0.80, Sp 0.90)
obs <- c(a = 27.8, c = 19.2, b = 48.2, d = 104.8)
a <- correct(obs["a"], 47, 0.80, 0.90)
b <- correct(obs["b"], 153, 0.80, 0.90)
rr <- (a / (a + b)) / ((47 - a) / (47 - a + 153 - b))
c(a = unname(a), b = unname(b), RR = unname(rr))
       est    lower    upper
1 2.930233 1.604305 5.352015
   point ci_limit 
5.308474 2.588931 
  est lower upper 
 2.20  1.20  4.01 
        a         b        RR 
33.000000 47.000000  3.535714

The first block is the MH RR with its Wald interval, 2.93 (1.60 to 5.35), as in §11.7. The E-values 5.31 and 2.59 are the confounder strengths needed to explain away the estimate and the lower limit. Dividing by the bounding factor 1.33 for an assumed (2, 2) confounder leaves 2.20 (1.20 to 4.01), still above 1. The last line recovers the true cells 33 and 47 and RR 3.54 from the misclassified table. The EValue and episensr packages automate these calculations but are not installed here; the base-R functions above are the whole method.

points.html: An E-value is not a test and not a probability. A large E-value says only that a strong confounder would be needed; whether one plausibly exists is a subject-matter judgement. Compare it with the strength of known confounders: here the rural PHC was 2.5 times as common among not-EBF infants (62.5% against 25.0%) and raised diarrhoea risk 1.67-fold among EBF infants (16.7% against 10.0%), both well short of 5.31.

The E-value is on the RR scale. It “can also be used for hazard ratios or odds ratios with outcomes that are rare at the end of follow-up” (Mathur et al., 2018); for an OR with a common outcome, such as the diarrhoea OR of 5.32 here (risk 23.5% overall), use the RR, or an approximate conversion.

Pre-specify sensitivity analyses in the protocol: complete-case against multiple imputation (recall §15.4.3), per-protocol against intention-to-treat (§15.9), and alternative definitions of exposure and outcome. Report them whether or not they agree.
Good practice for bias analysis is to state the bias model, justify the parameter values from validation data or literature, and present results over a range (Lash et al., 2014).

questions.prompt: Two studies each find no association between a workplace exposure and a health outcome. Study X sampled workers well but did not measure smoking, a known confounder. Study Y measured everything but recruited from a clinic that sees mainly workers who fell ill. Explain why these problems differ, how each could be addressed, and how each could have hidden a real effect.
questions.answer:
Study X has unmeasured confounding. Smoking was never recorded, so it cannot be adjusted for in these data. It can be addressed with new data (measure smoking, or a validation sub-sample), or bounded with a sensitivity analysis (§17.3.1): how strongly would smoking have to be related to exposure and outcome to change the conclusion? It could hide an effect if the confounding is negative: for example, if exposed workers smoke less than unexposed ones, and smoking raises the outcome risk, the harm of the exposure is offset.

Study Y has selection bias only if entry to the clinic depends on both exposure and outcome. Recruiting only workers who fell ill means everyone has, or is likely to have, the outcome; if exposed workers attend the clinic for exposure-related reasons as well, clinic attendance is a collider (§17.2.1) and the association among attenders can be pushed towards, or across, the null. No analysis of these data restores the missing workers; the fix is redesign (a cohort of all workers, or population-based cases and controls). Separately, a non-representative sample that did not depend on both would limit generalisability without biasing the association.

Both studies could also be affected by non-differential misclassification of exposure, which tends to push a real effect towards the null. “No association” is not “no effect” until these explanations are addressed.

questions.prompt: An adjusted RR is 1.8 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.7). Compute the E-values for the estimate and the confidence limit. Would a confounder with RR_EU = RR_UD = 2 explain the association away? (For a protective RR of 0.5, what is the E-value?)
questions.answer:
1. Estimate: 1.8 + √(1.8 × 0.8) = 1.8 + √1.44 = 1.8 + 1.2 = 3.0.
  2. Lower limit (closer to the null): 1.2 + √(1.2 × 0.2) = 1.2 + √0.24 = 1.2 + 0.49 = 1.69.
  3. Confounder (2, 2): B = 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33. Corrected RR ≥ 1.8 ÷ 1.33 = 1.35, corrected lower limit ≥ 1.2 ÷ 1.33 = 0.90. It cannot explain away the point estimate (2 < 3.0) but could explain away the lower limit (2 > 1.69): the interval could then include 1.
  4. Protective RR 0.5: invert to 2.0; E-value = 2 + √(2 × 1) = 2 + 1.41 = 3.41.

questions.prompt: A cohort adjusts for maternal education recorded only as “literate / not literate”, and an association remains. A colleague calls what remains “unmeasured confounding”. Correct her. Then name the three design-stage methods of controlling confounding and one limitation of each.
questions.answer:
Education was measured, but coarsely. What remains is residual confounding: differences in education within each of the two categories still confound. Recording years of schooling or finer categories would reduce it. Unmeasured confounding refers to a confounder never recorded.

Design-stage methods: (1) Randomisation: balances measured and unmeasured confounders on average, but only when the exposure can ethically and practically be assigned. (2) Restriction: admit one level of the confounder only; it cannot confound, but numbers fall and the result applies only to that level. (3) Matching: make comparison groups alike on the confounder; the analysis must account for the matching (in case-control studies matching alone does not remove confounding), and a matched variable’s own effect cannot then be studied.
